2 • WGA 2026 ANNUAL REPORT Dear Friends and Colleagues, Twice a year, during WGA’s Annual and Winter Meetings, Western Governors come together for a private dinner. There are no cameras or reporters, no industry or organization representatives – not even members of the Governors’ staff are present. Just the Governors and yours truly. In this relaxed setting, the titles and ceremony quickly fade away, and the room begins to feel less like a gathering of elected officials and more like a group of old friends swapping stories and passionately discussing the issues of the day. During the dinner, I am always struck by the genuine collegiality and fellowship around the table. In many ways, it feels like a family dinner during the holidays – complete with storytelling, spirited debate, and perhaps most importantly, a lot of laughter. At this year’s Annual Meeting in Deer Valley, Utah, Governor Spencer Cox said he wished the entire country could sit in on one of these dinners to see how the Governors – who come from very different backgrounds and political beliefs – discuss difficult issues with candor, respect, and a shared commitment to finding common ground. While these private gatherings tend to only happen at WGA’s Annual and Winter Meetings, the Governors actively meet with and support each other throughout the year. Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon traveled to Salt Lake City for the final workshop of Governor Cox’s WGA Chair initiative, Energy Superabundance: Unlocking Prosperity in the West. Idaho Governor Brad Little hosted Governor Cox at the Idaho National Laboratory for another Energy Superabundance workshop. New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham flew all the way to Maui for WGA’s 2026 Policy Forum where she spent two days talking with Hawaiʻi Governor Josh Green about disaster recovery. This year, thanks in part to Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs, Colorado Governor Jared Polis, and Governor Little – all of whom hosted workshops in support of Governor Cox’s WGA Chair initiative – WGA released an initiative report that includes a robust set of federal policy recommendations to expand the nation’s capacity for producing, transmitting, and storing energy. These reports don’t just look pretty and sit on the shelf. They have proven to be an effective mechanism for advancing western priorities in Washington, D.C. Several of the recommendations outlined in Governor Lujan Grisham’s WGA Chair initiative, Building Resilient and Affordable New Developments in the West (BRAND West), were incorporated in the recently enacted 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress also adopted policy recommendations related to the Carbon Dioxide Removal Purchase Pilot Prize program that were developed through Governor Gordon’s WGA Chair initiative, Decarbonizing the West. We expect similar results to stem from Governor Cox’s Energy Superabundance initiative. In addition to the initiative report, the Governors also approved 11 bipartisan policy resolutions this year on issues ranging from housing and broadband connectivity to permitting and agriculture. Summaries of all 11 resolutions can be found on pages 11 through 13 in this report. None of this work would be possible without the Governors’ commitment to working together to solve shared challenges. I want to especially thank Governor Cox for his outstanding leadership and stewardship as Chair this past year. His brand of politics is not only refreshing, but reflective of WGA’s proud bipartisan history of working together to accomplish great things for the region. As we welcome several new governors in the coming year, the Association could not be in better hands than those of its newly elected Chair, Hawaiʻi Governor Josh Green. Few leaders embody WGA’s bipartisan spirit more fully, and we look forward to carrying that spirit forward through his Chair initiative, Health Beyond Healthcare, while embracing the aloha spirit that defines his leadership. Of course, that means you will all have to come to WGA’s Winter Meeting on Oʻahu, Hawaiʻi, from December 10–12. The relationships the Western Governors have developed over the years have paved the way for meaningful policy that will have a lasting impact across the region for generations to come. This year’s gathering was no different, and we expect more storytelling, more spirited debate, and yes, more laughter, in the year ahead. Jack Waldorf WGA Executive Director

4 • WGA 2026 ANNUAL REPORT EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Utah Governor Spencer Cox, as Chair of the Western Governors’ Association, launched the Energy Superabundance: Unlocking Prosperity in the West initiative in July 2025.  The initiative examined challenges and opportunities for expanding production, transmission, and storage options across the energy spectrum to unlock more reliable, secure, and affordable energy to meet growing demand and achieve energy abundance across the West. The West is rich in diverse energy resources, offering significant opportunities for both traditional and renewable energy development.  Vast reserves of oil, natural gas, coal, and hydropower; high-quality wind, solar, nuclear, and geothermal resources; and plentiful critical mineral deposits position western states as leaders in both energy production and innovation. The initiative examined many key elements of energy development, from energy resources and supply chain challenges to electricity generation and transmission, as well as workforce development and permitting issues. Despite our immense resource abundance, growing energy demand driven by factors like changing populations, the increased  electrification of our society, and the proliferation of energy- intensive industries like artificial intelligence, is adding strain to our current electricity systems. Achieving energy abundance will require more energy from a broader spectrum of energy sources. The viability and opportunity for different types of energy  generation varies across states and applications.  While there are numerous methods of energy production, collaborative work on transmission stands out as an area where the West can realize an important benefit.  UNLOCKING PROSPERITY IN THE WEST The Initiative of Utah Governor Spencer Cox

# Page 5^page=5
WGA 2026 ANNUAL REPORT • 5 Permitting and regulatory challenges are also key aspects of achieving energy superabundance.  Inefficient and cumbersome permitting processes significantly hinder the development of energy projects by creating delays, increasing costs, and adding uncertainty to investments.  These barriers slow the deployment of energy resources, preventing critical infrastructure from keeping pace with growing demand.  Streamlining permitting and modernizing regulations are essential elements to accelerating energy development and ensuring a more resilient and abundant energy system. Western Governors contributed their personal resources and effort to the initiative by hosting workshops in their states.  WGA is especially indebted to these workshop hosts: Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs, Colorado Governor Jared Polis, Idaho Governor Brad Little, and Utah Governor Spencer Cox.  The workshop sessions are available for viewing on WGA’s YouTube page, and additional information about the initiative can be found at WGA’s website. The initiative received an enormous amount of input from a wide variety of interested stakeholders, including state and federal energy experts, private businesses, and non- governmental organizations.  The report developed as a result of the Energy Superabundance: Unlocking Prosperity in the West initiative incorporates these stakeholders’ consensus recommendations to put western states on a path toward a future of energy superabundance that is reliable, secure, and affordable – a future that provides our western communities with the energy they need for unbridled economic opportunity and improved quality of life.  The efforts of the Energy Superabundance: Unlocking Prosperity in the West initiative establish a solid foundation to address some of the most challenging aspects of achieving energy superabundance.  Western Governors encourage federal decision makers and our partners to implement these recommendations and work to secure an environmentally responsible, affordable, and abundant energy future for the West.  Utah Governor Spencer Cox hosted the final workshop for his WGA Chair initiative, Energy Superabundance: Unlocking Prosperity in the West, in Salt Lake City, Utah.

6 • WGA 2026 ANNUAL REPORT POLICY PROGRESS Western Governors take a strongly bipartisan, common-sense approach to address the most pressing policy challenges in the West.  This bipartisan ethic is proving to be effective in Washington, D.C., as Western Governors’ policy shows practical paths forward while much of the nation is mired in partisan division.   Over the past year, WGA shared Western Governors’ bipartisan policy recommendations with federal agencies and Congress on 37 rulemakings and pieces of legislation. Topics ranged from permitting and housing to workforce development and land management. Many of those recommendations have since been reflected in federal policy, with agencies incorporating Governors’ priorities into regulatory frameworks and organizational structures. Congress has also taken steps to advance Governors’ policy through federal statutes. The federal actions listed below provide a brief description of how Western Governors’ policy priorities were incorporated into federal policy. COMMUNITY & OPPORTUNITY   Housing 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: The bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law in July 2026, implements key recommendations from New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham’s WGA Chair initiative, Building Resilient and Affordable New Developments in the West (BRAND West). This includes provisions designed to increase housing development in Opportunity Zones, eliminate the permanent chassis requirement for manufactured homes, reauthorize the HOME Investment Partnerships Program, and make reforms to U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Rural Housing Service programs by decoupling rental assistance from maturing mortgages. (Public Law 119-101) Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC): Congress expanded the LIHTC program – the primary federal financing tool for affordable rental housing – by permanently increasing the state allocation cap for 9 percent credits by 12 percent, starting in fiscal year 2026, lowering the private activity bond financing threshold from 50 percent to 25 percent, and providing a 30 percent basis boost for projects in rural and tribal communities. These changes are intended to provide states with greater financing flexibility and accelerate the preservation and development of affordable housing, particularly in underserved areas. (Public Law 119-21)  Removing Regulatory Barriers to Affordable Housing Construction: To reduce regulatory, permitting, and financing barriers on housing development, President Trump issued an executive order that focuses on streamlining federal processes and promoting the development of single- family, modular, and manufactured housing. (Executive Order 14394)   Agriculture   House Farm Bill: The House passed the Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026, also known as the 2026 Farm Bill, which reflects many of Western Governors’ agriculture policy priorities, including the authorization of programs related to specialty crop assistance, the farm safety net, conservation, and critical agricultural research programs.  (H.R. 7567) Western Governors at WGA’s 2025 Winter Meeting in Scottsdale, Arizona, spoke with Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services, also provided a keynote.

# Page 7^page=7
WGA 2026 ANNUAL REPORT • 7 Rural Development   Secure Rural Schools: Congress reauthorized the Secure Rural Schools program, which provides federal funding to rural counties to support schools, roads, and essential services in areas with significant federally owned land. It also provided the past two years of lapsed payments. (Public Law 119-58)  Payment in Lieu of Taxes (PILT): Congress fully funded PILT, which provides federal payments to local governments that help offset losses in property taxes due to the presence of nontaxable federal lands within their boundaries. (Public Law 119-74)  Workforce Workforce Pell Grants: To expand access to training that leads to in-demand jobs,  Congress expanded eligibility for Pell Grants to include  high-quality, short-term,  workforce-oriented programs. (Public Law 119-21) ENERGY & ENVIRONMENT   Air Quality  Promoting Prescribed Fire: After engaging with Western Governors, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) issued guidance directing its regional offices to work with their state partners to address regulatory barriers for the expanded deployment of prescribed fire. While this guidance is focused on the implementation of the Exceptional Events Rule, the agency is also taking additional actions to promote prescribed fire via the Regional Haze rule and other pathways. Energy Carbon Dioxide Removal:  The Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) Purchase Pilot Prize, which is a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) competition designed to accelerate the development of high-quality carbon dioxide removal technologies and markets by enabling companies to sell verified CDR credits directly to the federal government, was  allocated $45 million this year. (Public Law 119-37)   • Of that funding, $4 million will be used to develop measurement, monitoring, reporting, and verification (MMRV) standards that will inform the purchase prize, offtake agreements, and other federal incentives.  • Congress also restructured the Section 45Q Tax Credit for carbon capture and sequestration to provide equal credit value, regardless of whether carbon is sequestered, utilized, or used for enhanced oil recovery.      Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon stands in front of the Dry Fork Station just outside of Gillette, Wyoming, where the state tests carbon capture technology. Several of the policy recommendations in his WGA Chair initiative, Decarbonizing the West, were adopted by Congress this year. The Energy Superabundance workshop at the Idaho National Laboratory featured a discussion on workforce development in the nuclear energy industry with Bethany Coates, Chief Executive Officer at BreakLine; Michelle Fussell, Legislative Representative at Iron Workers International; Chris Hayter, COO & Co-Founder of of Hi Tech Solutions; and Jimmy McDonough; Assistant Commissioner for the State of Utah Education Workforce Programs.

8 • WGA 2026 ANNUAL REPORT Mining   Good Samaritan Pilot Program: Following the passage of the Good Samaritan Remediation of Abandoned Hardrock Mines Act of 2024, EPA has worked to launch the Good Samaritan Pilot Program – which will allow certain individuals or organizations to undertake remediation without facing environmental liability risks – by establishing guidance for financial assurance requirements and working with state, tribal, and federal partners to develop and define future permitting processes for pilot program applicants. (Public Law 118-155) • EPA also established the Good Samaritan Mine Remediation Fund within the U.S. Treasury to allow the Good Samaritan Program to receive funds through appropriations, reprocessing proceeds, and other mechanisms to facilitate improved annual resource plan development.   EPA plans to launch the first of  three phases of program implementation later this year.    Minerals Mapping: Congress maintained FY24 funding levels for the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, which was launched to modernize the nation’s surface and subsurface mapping with a focus on critical mineral resources. (Public Law 119-74)  Water Water Forecasting: The Snow Survey and Water Supply Forecasting Program, which supplies snowpack measurements, precipitation data, and seasonal water supply forecasts to support water management in the western United States, was allotted $16.7 million, $2 million more than FY25. (Public Law 119-37)  State and Tribal Assistance Grants (STAG): STAGs are a crucial tool that enable states to execute their environmental management duties under federal environmental statutes.  They are EPA’s operational mechanism for cooperative federalism, and they fund a spectrum of management activities across environmental domains.  This year, Congress rejected a proposal to eliminate STAGs and instead appropriated $3.6 billion to the account, which is $27 million more than FY25 enacted funding levels. (Public Law 119-74)  A map created by the Snow Survey and Water Supply Forecasting Program on July 9, 2026, that depicts precipitation levels by basin.

WGA 2026 ANNUAL REPORT • 9 HEALTH & PUBLIC SAFETY   Disaster  Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC): Pre-disaster mitigation and risk reduction are among the most cost-effective ways to protect lives, property, infrastructure, and the environment from natural and human-caused hazards. On March 25, 2026, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) reinstated the BRIC program, a major federal grant initiative supporting infrastructure and hazard mitigation projects that reduce disaster risk and strengthen community resilience. Health Care Indian Health Service (IHS):  Responsible for providing direct medical and public health services for American Indians and Alaska Natives, IHS received $5.31 billion in advance appropriations for FY27 — a $72.8 million increase over FY26 advance appropriations. (Public Law 119-74) Rural Health Transformation Program: Established by the FY26 Budget Reconciliation Act, the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program will provide states and territories with funding to improve health and well-being in rural communities by prioritizing the rural clinical workforce, rural health infrastructure and technology, care coordination, and payment reform. (Public Law 119-21)      Radiation Exposure Compensation:  Congress reauthorized and expanded the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (RECA) to compensate individuals who contracted certain cancers and other serious diseases after exposure to radiation released from atmospheric nuclear weapons tests or following occupational exposure to radiation while employed in the uranium industry. (Public Law 119-21) Great American Recovery Initiative: 48.4 million Americans, or 17 percent of the U.S. population, suffer from substance use disorder (SUD). Many of these people, however, do not receive the care they need.  To coordinate a national response to the disease of addiction, President Trump launched the Addressing Addiction Through the Great American Recovery Initiative to increase awareness and advise agencies on implementing programs and grants related to SUD.  (Executive Order 14379)    DEA Telehealth Extension: The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) jointly with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued the Fourth Temporary Extension of COVID-19 Telehealth Flexibilities for Prescription of Controlled Medications. The rule extends the ability for practitioners to remotely prescribe controlled substances to patients, without an in-person medical evaluation, through December 31, 2026.   (90 FR 61301)    Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. spoke with Western Governors at WGA’s 2025 Winter Meeting in Scottsdale, Arizona, about rebuilding public trust through greater scientific transparency and collaboration with Governors.

(Public Law 119-37) Smoke Exposure: Congress encouraged  EPA to expand its support for smoke monitoring in areas with sparse monitoring infrastructure and directed it to reduce the administrative burden on states and tribes that use the Exceptional Events Rule for prescribed burns. • Western Governors also advocated for the Fire Improvement and Reforming Exceptional Events Act, or the FIRE Act, which passed the House. Hazard Pay for Prescribed Fire: To help recruit and retain an effective land management and wildland firefighting workforce, the U.S. Office of Personnel and Management issued a proposed rule which, if finalized, would provide additional “hazard pay” for federal employees conducting prescribed burns.   (91 FR 19081) Landscapes  Grazing Allotments:  Congress directed the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and USFS to make vacant grazing allotments available to a holder of a grazing permit or lease when that permittee’s lands are unusable due to drought or wildfire. (Public Law 119-74)   • Congress also provided funding to address the backlog of allotments still requiring  National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) analyses. LAND MANAGEMENT   Forestry and Fire U.S. Forest Service State Directors: USDA released its department reorganization plan in July 2025. In March 2026, after corresponding with Western Governors who recommended that transitioning the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) to a state-based organizational model would provide an essential conduit for state-federal coordination on land management, USDA announced that the USFS would transition to a State Director model. Forestry in the Farm Bill: The Forestry title in the 2026 Farm Bill that was passed by the House this year reflects nearly every Farm Bill policy priority regarding forestry that WGA recommended to Congress.  These priorities include reforming the Good Neighbor Authority, supporting reforestation supply chains, incentivizing forest restoration activity through biomass utilization grants, and more. (H.R. 7567)     • Additionally, the 2026 Farm Bill incorporates provisions from the Fix Our Forests Act, elements of which WGA has also been supportive of, including improvements to Shared Stewardship agreements, expanding the use of prescribed fire, and the establishment of fireshed management project strike teams with the express purpose of accelerating environmental review, site preparation, and project implementation. Immediately afterwards, he joined a panel discussion with the Governors about how states and the federal government can more effectively partner to mitigate wildfire risk.

WGA 2026 ANNUAL REPORT • 11 Western Governors formally approved 11 policy resolutions in FY26. 14 • WGA 2026 ANNUAL REPORT 2025 WINTER MEETING It’s roughly 2,300 miles from Washington, D.C., to Scottsdale, Arizona, where the Western Governors’ Association held its 2025 Winter Meeting. However, listening to the bipartisan discussions there, you’d have thought the two cities were worlds apart. “One of the best parts of these gatherings is that political labels tend to fade away,” WGA’s Chair, Utah Governor Spencer Cox, said. “While we certainly don’t agree on everything, and you will see some robust disagreement, I think many of those who attend these meetings leave with a renewed sense of camaraderie and faith in the power of bipartisanship. My hope is that over the next few days, the rest of the country can see that same spirit in action and be reminded that working together actually still works.”  “We really are trying to find common ground,” WGA’s Vice Chair, Hawaiʻi Governor Josh Green, added. “There’s not as much of that in Washington, D.C. but in the Governors’ Association, it really is collegial… and I think today you’ll see it in action.” Joining Governor Cox and Governor Green at this year’s Winter Meeting were Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs, Idaho Governor Brad Little, Montana Governor Greg Gianforte, and New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham. In addition to panel discussions about the energy needs for data centers, broadband expansion, and the Farm Bill, the attending Governors also spoke with Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum and Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “I like to think of Western Governors’ Association as not just the group that’s developing state or regional policy,” Secretary Burgum said, “but in many cases, it’s the policies that have been formed right here in this room by the teams, the staffs, the Governors’ staffs, that actually shape the direction of this country.”   From left to right: Idaho Governor Brad Little, Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs, Utah Governor Spencer Cox, Hawaiʻi Governor Josh Green, and Montana Governor Greg Gianforte at the 2025 Winter Meeting in Scottsdale, Arizona. # Page 15^page=15
WGA 2026 ANNUAL REPORT • 15 2026 ANNUAL MEETING Ahead of the America 250 celebration, bipartisanship was on full display at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Western Governors’ Association in beautiful Deer Valley, Utah. “One of the things that always gives me hope as I talk about our country is every time I have the opportunity to be together with my fellow Governors – some red, some blue, some purple – we come together in a bipartisan spirit,” WGA’s Chair and the host of the 2026 Annual Meeting, Utah Governor Spencer Cox, said.  “We had a dinner last night, and I wish that America could have been there. What you would have seen is dear friends having a great time talking about hard issues… When we take time to talk to each other and get to know each other better, we find that we all face the same challenges, we’re all working to find common-sense, practical solutions, and meetings like this give us an opportunity to do that – to learn from each other, to exchange ideas, to look for common ground, and to benefit from our collective experiences and wisdom.” This spirit of bipartisanship carried through to the many in-depth policy discussions that the Governors led at this year’s Annual Meeting. For these discussions, Governor Cox was joined by WGA’s Vice Chair, Hawai’i Governor Josh Green, as well as Colorado Governor Jared Polis, Idaho Governor Brad Little, Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo, New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, and Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon. The meeting began with Governor Cox releasing a report culminating his WGA Chair initiative, Energy Superabundance: Unlocking Prosperity in the West. The report summarizes the key issues that were explored during the initiative workshops in Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, and Utah, and presents federal policy recommendations developed from those discussions to help plan, finance, develop, and deploy energy projects across the West. Immediately following the release of the report, the Governors hosted a panel discussion to examine the report’s recommendations with experts from the DOE Office of Energy Dominance Financing, the Idaho National Laboratory, the Western Transmission Expansion Coalition (WestTEC), and Fervo Energy. “We live in an age of miracles, and every one of those miracles needs an electron,” Governor Cox said during the panel. “Because when an electron touches a hospital, lives are saved. When an electron touches a school, ideas come to fruition, and wisdom is learned. When an electron touches a home, families flourish. By definition, we have to work together if we’re going to get those electrons where they need to go, and if we’re going to lower prices for the people who call our states home and make life easier and more abundant so that human flourishing can actually happen at levels that we’ve never experienced before.” Next up was a keynote address from U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz, who emphasized the urgent need for active, collaborative forest management as the West faces an increasingly severe wildfire season. Building upon his keynote, Chief Schultz joined panelists from the Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation, the Colorado Department of Natural Resources, and the National Wild Turkey Federation for a discussion about how Shared Stewardship agreements are redefining land management and fire mitigation to the benefit of our states and the federal government. From left to right: Idaho Governor Brad Little, Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon, Utah Governor Spencer Cox, New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, Hawaiʻi Governor Josh Green, Colorado Governor Jared Polis, and Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo at the 2026 Annual Meeting in Deer Valley, Utah.

16 • WGA 2026 ANNUAL REPORT WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT That evening, the Governors were joined by the President of the Swiss Confederation, Guy Parmelin, who spoke about the close ties between Switzerland and western states and the great opportunities that exist to strengthen ties between our two countries. The Governors also heard from Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll about some of the challenges facing the United States and the important role Governors have in protecting our national security. Day two of WGA’s Annual Meeting featured panels on protecting state technology ecosystems from foreign influence, FEMA reform, and student literacy, the latter of which was led by Utah First Lady Abby Cox. “None of the biggest problems that we need to solve are going to be solved if we do not look towards the next generation and make sure that our kiddos have what they need to be successful,” First Lady Cox said. “And that means literacy.” The meeting concluded with Governor Cox handing the reins as the Chair of WGA to Governor Green. “It’s just with extreme gratitude that I get to participate with these great people and all of you,” Governor Green said. “We genuinely love this work, as you can tell, and we look forward to doing it with you in the coming months and many years ahead.” As the newly elected Chair, Governor Green announced the launch of his WGA Chair initiative, Health Beyond Healthcare, which will focus on improving mental health outcomes by expanding access to care while addressing the broader factors that shape health and well-being. “Access to healthcare is one of the defining challenges facing the West,” said Governor Green. “But health doesn’t begin in a doctor’s office. It begins where we live, learn, work, and play. Through this initiative, we have an opportunity to work together across state lines to improve access to care, strengthen our communities and advance practical, bipartisan solutions that improve lives.” To learn more about the Health Beyond Healthcare initiative and get involved, visit WGA’s website. 2026 POLICY FORUM In recent years, Hawaiʻi Governor Josh Green and New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham have been at the forefront of response and recovery efforts following some of the region’s most significant disasters. WGA’s 2026 Policy Forum featured Governors Green and Lujan Grisham in a discussion about the lessons that they’ve learned from those experiences, as well as strategies that they think can help communities better prepare for, respond to, and recover from future disasters. The two-day workshop, hosted just a few miles from the newly rebuilt town of Lahaina, Hawaiʻi, also convened disaster response experts from around the country for panels about lessons from the Lahaina wildfire, rebuilding after disasters, trauma-informed approaches to disaster recovery, the future of disaster management and recovery, and disaster recovery in rural communities. “I know that you’ve heard many of the stories,” Governor Green said, “but we wanted to bring people with expertise to share what our experience was so that you can take best practices away or areas where we can improve. That’s what we’re about.” “I want to give Hawaiʻi and Governor Green a shoutout,” Governor Lujan Grisham said. “I thought it was really effective the way in which you’re leveraging both private dollars and state dollars so that you just built a community (for wildfire survivors)... I’m going to steal that model, which is exactly why I’m here.”  Hawaiʻi Governor Josh Green and New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham led a discussion at WGA’s 2026 Policy Forum about disaster preparedness and response.

A final workshop will be hosted in Hawaiʻi, though an exact date has not been set yet.
